utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly remind the witness she is still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms Calic, you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we are still in cross-examination. Ms Residovic, continue where you stopped. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. During the cross-examination yesterday I had reached the chapter on the region of Konjic and Mrs Calic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you hold on because we are having nothing on the screen, on the transcript. What is happening? (Pause). You can continue now. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. I will continue with questions referring to the announced subject matter by the prosecution and the expert witness, and that has to do with the historical, political, civilian and military element of the structure of the town of Konjic. Good morning, Ms Calic. Before I resume my questions I should like to apologise to you if some of my questions yesterday were a bit strict. Not one of those questions was designed against you personally, but rather the subject-matter of interest to my client, and I hope you will understand that after four years of horror in Sarajevo, we may be a little more emotional than otherwise. May I continue then? Yesterday afternoon I asked you which were the sources of your knowledge about Konjic, and you told me that unfortunately you did not have many documents that you received only a limited number of documents from the prosecution, and that you are lacking documents about Konjic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I used different sources, official data books published. I used also the reports by the international experts' commission by the UN, which are also included in this file, but I was also using some documents provided by yourself and also by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that you did not have at your disposal a large number of documents of the official authorities of the town of Konjic to be able to preside a full expert opinion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have liked to have some more official data which were requested, but for some mysterious reasons the authorities or the respective officers in Sarajevo were not able to provide me with these documents, but they maybe will come out with them. We keep on trying to get them.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am sure you will agree with me that the mysterious reasons include the four-year war, because for ten months of the investigations I could not get hold of many documents myself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This may be, but there were also other official data, like population censuses, and other quite official data which could not be provided by the officers in Sarajevo. I had to go through OAC and other institutes, I am afraid. It was a very difficult research to get even very basic documents.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we could agree that your knowledge of Konjic on the basis of the documents you had is limited by the quantity of documents you disposed of, and that the conclusions you made in this report and which I have commented on would not be up to the standard that a doctor of history, historical sciences, would like to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can always find more documents and more documents, and I think I have seen quite a broad range, a wide range of different documents on this area. Of course, if I continue to do research, I will find ever more documents, and I think I had quite a good overview on what happened in Konjic. I am, of course, not a fact witness. I have emphasised this yesterday many times, and for this reason there are also other witnesses coming here to give evidence on what they have seen in the area. I, of course, was not there at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will not ask you anything about any event that would require your personal knowledge of an event as an eye witness, but could you please show us document number 50 from your binder? Can we see this document, please, number 50? Would you agree with me that this document, which you yourself said that you compiled, is not well-founded or is poorly founded on official documents, or did you have those documents in mind when you made this drawing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had indeed documents in mind when I did this drawing. I knew from the documents that there was a War Presidency. I knew from the documents that there was an HVO and a TO, Bosnian Army headquarters in Konjic. I knew from the documents that they were interrelated and they had a joint command and I also knew from the documents that there was a coordination instance, and all these informations were perfectly in line with what I knew from strategy of all people's defence from Jugoslavia and on the strategy of all people's defence in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question, whether the documents which refer to this drawing that you have made, in addition to the official documents, such as laws and others, were these documents given to you by the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were given to me by the prosecution, and some of them were given by the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the defence did not give you a single document, nor did we have any contact with you. All that we gave, we have given to the prosecution, and therefore all the documents that you received must have been from the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there were documents which I received from the Office of the Prosecutor which were coming evidently from the defence. This is what I understood, where these documents were coming from, and I used several of them.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From Zejnil Delalic's defence counsel you did not receive anything in person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in person, but I saw several documents which had your name on the top of the paper, so I was convinced that these documents were submitted by the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us the document on the basis of which you reached such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can show you these documents if you give me the time to pick them up in my office, and they are based on several documents.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are they contained in the binder that you have submitted to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are not all contained. Some of them are contained in the binder, as far as the War Presidency is concerned. As far as the military structures are concerned, they are contained in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to allow me to come back to this question if you can bring those documents during the break, and now I will proceed. Did you have in mind the statute of the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have in mind the rules of procedure of the War Presidency of the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you already said that you bore in mind the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you agree with me that the structures in Konjic were formed in accordance with the documents which the municipality of Konjic had before the war, and the documents which the competent authorities passed after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle yes, but from March onwards I got the impression that the administrative bodies in the municipality of Konjic did not function any more the way they functioned the months before. This was, of course, due to the difficult situation in this country, but I would not agree that they were perfectly in line with the laws passed before the war just because a part of members of the Assembly had left the Assembly, and they were not represented in the War Presidency according to the law, because the Bosnian law from before the war said that certain members should be represented, and these members were not represented any more. So there was a certain gap between what was on paper and what was on reality, and there are, of course, reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The impression that you had on the method of work of the local bodies is that your personal impression or a scientific impression, based on documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is based on documents.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have explained that a number of members of bodies had left those bodies. Are you aware of the legal regulations for filling in the vacancies after certain people ceased to be members of the Assembly or other municipal bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware, and this brings me somehow back to the questions you put yesterday to me, I am aware of the fact that in democratic countries, once the elected bodies do not function any more, there should be new elections to form new bodies, and this was not the case, neither on the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor in the municipalities, on the local level.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not ask you for any abstract country. I asked you about our country, where there is a law on elections, and which regulated the situation when the need arose to substitute members of the government or the Presidency, if for some reason they ceased to perform those duties. Are you familiar with those regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was your impression based on those regulations or on some others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My analysis was based on what appeared to have happened on the ground, and I would like to emphasise again that there is a big difference between what was written on paper and what was written in these laws, and what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you said that you were not there, and that you had a lack of documents from the spot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not personally there, but I saw many, many documents giving evidence on exactly this fact.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your report you said that from April 1992 the TO of Konjic formed a joint command with the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a single document to confirm that in April such a joint command was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please do so? If I say that the joint command was formed on 12th May, do you consider that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Maybe I did not understand your question very well. This document says clearly here May. I did not speak about April. I know that there was a joint command. I put on my diagram the date of May, not of April. Maybe I did not get your question very well. So let's stay with May. I can bring you the document.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if it says in my translation that as of April 1992 a joint command was formed, then that is incorrect, incorrectly stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just bring the document and check, if you allow.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you please show us the document number 23 from your file? It is a decree abolishing the republican staff of Territorial Defence and forming a territorial staff headquarters of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a Decision on the proclamation of an immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before that on the same page there is a decree abolishing the former republican headquarters of TO and forming the TO headquarters of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I not right? That is the first decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but we have not translated it, so it might be a problem for the judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what I was wondering. It is not there. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): That decree speaks of the structure of the defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but, you see, there is a problem. I wanted to use the document on the decision on the proclamation of an immediate threat of war and this document is here in the translation but not the other one which happened to be on the same page in the original document. So we don't have it in translation and it may be difficult just now to argue on that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms Calic, this one has to do with the defence forces of the republic, and I have been informed that you will be discussing that too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can discuss this issue too, of course, but it makes no sense to put this document now here on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at paragraph 2? Will you please read that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But the rest of us may not be familiar, so will you please read it for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe we can have an official translation. I would not like to translate it here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will read it nevertheless: "The Ministry of National Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina through the staff of Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina conducts and commands the structures of Territorial Defence." Do you consider this to be a significant decision taken on 9th April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a significant decision taken.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the next day the Ministry of Defence passed a decree regulating the method of proceeding in Territorial Defence staffs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the bodies in the Konjic municipality acted in accordance with these decisions of the competent bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't actually know if they were able to do so, because the communication lines between Sarajevo and Konjic appeared to be interrupted at that time, so I don't know to which extent, and I was trying to explain this yesterday, I actually do not know to which extent the laws and decrees and decisions taken in Sarajevo came through to Konjic and to which extent they were actually implemented. I do not know this.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but even though you do not know that, which I accept, you have nevertheless claimed that the composition and competence of the newly-formed municipal institutions was unclear and diverse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was for the very same reason unclear to me who exactly participated in the work of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your report on your expert opinion you said this: in the course of April and May 1992 armed conflicts occurred between the TO and the HVO, on the one hand, and the JNA and the Serb side on the other in the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms Calic, do you know that in mid-April Konjic was blocked entirely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mentioned this already yesterday, and I tried to explain yesterday that I did not witness personally such blocking of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive some documents from the prosecution referring to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw some documents referring to blocking of towns and also of armed conflict around this town. I actually got also the final report of the commission of experts from the UN telling us about some of the events happening, and I did not introduce this document, but I might introduce it today. It is document number 55. It tells us about also different paramilitary forces coming in and how these armed conflicts started. So this is in my view a reliable source and this is why I included it in this binder. I, of course, have no possibility to check whether or not the witness statements are true or not. I have no opportunity -- I had no opportunity so far to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a general objection to this line of questioning. It goes, as far as I can understand, to the factual things that happened in Konjic on certain dates of blocking, etc. The purpose of bringing Dr Calic here as an expert witness is to give a general overview of the background to these charges we are going to try in this trial, and I cannot see -- I must object to the defence attempt to have Mrs Calic to bring in every document on which she actually relied. She is giving answers to every question put to her, but when we go into certain factual things that happened in Konjic, this is not her duty to answer it and she cannot and should not and has not been asked. It is not her task when we asked her to come here to appear as an expert witness. I object to the factual questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, Delalic is being charged with the command possibility. The witness has talked about the composition of the forces there of both sides. She has talked about what is happening there. So maybe the question is relevant in the sense that she wants to say there is complete confusion, and the commander could not be held responsible for what had been done anywhere else in that area. The witness has spoken about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But nevertheless, your Honour, these last questions, many of these questions are really factual questions, what happened on the ground. That is not what Dr Calic is here to answer. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I think that I have the right to verify the knowledge and the views of the expert witness, especially as in her report the witness mentions dates and events. I have just repeated what she has written in her report, April, May 1992. Please allow me to continue the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can question the witness, but try to avoid roving questions which might not be useful to you. They sometimes may be counter-productive. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Ms Calic, are you aware that the town of Konjic at the time of the events and before the events described in the indictment that you have seen was attacked from Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see from the report which I put on the ELMO that there were attacks from different sides at different times. So as I am not a fact witness and I was not on the ground at this time, I could not judge here or I could not confirm, and not confirm which of these contradictory reports are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Has the prosecution given you access to the documentation on the arming of the Serbian population which was submitted to us by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I also included one of these reports, which, by the way, I found myself, and it was not given to me by the Office of the Prosecutors in this file. I also stressed this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to another question. You stated that the HVO and the TO operated under the command structures that were separated from the civilian structures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stated that there was no direct subordination, but they were parallel structures, but they were, of course, interlinked and they were acting together and they were having obviously meetings, and they were also taking joint decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the HVO structures throughout this period were under the direct authority of the para-state authorities of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know this. They had a separate headquarters on the territory of the Herceg-Bosna para-state.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have all documents relating to the HVO in possession of the prosecutor been made available to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Based on a document on the establishment of Herceg-Bosna from 1991, did you know that within that para-state structure the municipality of Konjic was also included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I showed this yesterday even here on the screen. I submitted this document. I explained exactly this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She has already said that yesterday about the Croatians' sort of plan. They wanted to include Konjic was part of their territory. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): From those documents was the Konjic municipality also included within the borders of this community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I submitted yesterday a document showing that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna were laying claim to the territory of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your report you stated that the HVO had no interest in fighting in other areas, because there was not enough Croatian population in those areas. Please can you tell us: was this goal realised in Ivan Sedlo and Konjic area, was this aim realised, that they wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you please kindly -- the Trial Chamber will rise for just a few minutes. Just about ten minutes. (10.35 am) (Short break) (10.50 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please continue from now. You will not lose your ten or fifteen minutes. You will get it back. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Ms Calic, I apologise for a little confusion on the document number 50. Would you please repeat this document was made by you yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 50?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, number 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 50 was done by myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, that is not an official document by anybody? It is your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document which I did on the basis of the documents I have seen and of my expertise. It thus became a document, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You presented the tactical group in your report; is that correct, and you quoted the Military Encyclopedia, which is document number 36 in your binder; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I quoted two official documents, the Military Encyclopaedia and the Military Lexicon.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also take into account the regulations of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, because I am not a military person, and there will be another expert explaining all the details of the military formations. I am here to give a general background and a very general explanation on what tactical groups were. How they were functioning in detail and how they were functioning at this time is not within my field of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These documents, you do not have information on the date of the establishment of the tactical groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have these documents available.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if in your report there are precise dates of when the tactical groups were established, then that information is not based on this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had various sources telling that there were tactical groups established, one of them being tactical group number one acting in the direction of Sarajevo, but I have not seen any documents that referred concretely to any date when these tactical groups were established and how they were composed and who commanded them. This is why I remained a bit vague in my report. I just wanted to introduce the fact that there were tactical groups, and I wanted to explain in a very general way what these tactical groups were meant to be.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you only saw the document on the establishment of tactical group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I saw various sources telling me that there were several tactical groups established during this time acting in different directions. I made not only studies on the municipality of Konjic but also in other areas of Bosnia, and I came across several times this phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms Calic, according to your documents these tactical groups were temporary joined formations that were operating in a particular direction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were established to fulfil a very specific purpose, as I explained, supported by the Military Lexicon in the article I presented yesterday here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If in your report other tasks of a tactical group are also mentioned, that means it is not based on what you provided as the basic document defining the tactical group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic document defining the tactical groups comes from 1981 and the Military Encyclopaedia, I think from 1976, so, of course, these two documents that explain in a very general way what a tactical group is could not include any detailed information on tactical groups which were established in 1992, but, as I was saying before, I saw many documents referring to the fact that there were tactical groups established and this had also concrete composition, but as I am not a military person, I cannot explain exactly who, how, why and who commanded it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question was not about the command. It was about the establishment; in other words, you do not know when the tactical groups 1, 2, 3, operation group Igman and others, were established which had a task of lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not use any document which referred to an exact date of establishment of any tactical group, but this was also not within my mandate to elaborate on these very concrete military things. I am not an expert in war, so I am giving here the general background, and as for the specific questions, there may be documents. I have not used them in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms Calic, I will only mention that my client is charged as Commander of the tactical group 1. I thought that you may have some more accurate data about when this tactical group was established, because that was within the task that the prosecutor said would be part of your expertise, but if you do not know about that, I will not insist on further questions in that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, for information for the court, as I mentioned in our opening statement, in our witness statement is General De Vogel, who has been a military attache to Belgrade. If necessary, as I said, he will be called to answer details on the tactical group, its commands, etc. I ask Ms Residovic to reserve her questions until he appears. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, maybe I would not have asked these questions if the prosecution opening did not contain comments that someone may be called if necessary. If the Prosecutor deems it is not necessary and given that the facts that this witness is testifying to are of interest to us, I thought that I needed to ask these questions. So I am not continuing my questioning on the tactical group. You based your expertise on the given data that you had, and so these are the documents that formed the basis of your opinion in that area. I will only ask for one minute so that I can move on to another area, and I would like to locate that document. As everything is all right with the equipment, I would ask that we hear the tape that we were unable to hear yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object on the ground of relevance. I cannot see the relevance of that tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I do not see the necessity of introducing it now. As I pointed out yesterday, this witness has no connection with that. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I would like to ask you, Mr President, to abide by yesterday's decision, because the questions I am going to ask are directly linked to this tape, and to the witness' testimony on the events. The recording is only 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually the witness has answered all you asked her yesterday, and I thought that was conclusive of the questions you wanted to know. Have you other questions to ask? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): As it was not possible to hear the sound, I could not ask all the questions, and this is a historical fact and an event that had a decisive impact on developments in various places, including the municipality of Konjic. I, therefore, ask you, your Honours, to allow us to hear and see the tape so that I may ask some more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I do not enjoy dialogues of this nature. I have told you exactly what the position is. Please go on and ask other questions, if you have any. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Ms Calic, in your report you said that you were aware of certain speculations linked to the meeting between Tudjman and Milosevic and Karadzic; is that correct, on the division of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read several reports in the press about possible meetings between the two and between possible alleged agreements on the division of Bosnia between Croatian and Serbia, but I have not seen any document confirming such agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned this, you had in mind Mr Fanjo Tudjman, the then and still President of the Republic of Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among others.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mean Fanjo Tudjman is just one, among others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there was also speculation that other persons made such agreements, whether or not they were in a position to make such agreements, but there was speculation widespread.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of all of us and since those names are cited in your report, will you please identify them? When you mentioned Tudjman, you had in mind Mr Fanjo Tudjman, the President of Croatia. When you mentioned Milosevic, you had in mind Slobodan Milosevic, the President of Serbia. When you mentioned the meeting with Boban, you were thinking of Mate Boban, President of the so-called Herceg-Bosna, a para-state in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When you mentioned Karadzic, you had in mind Radovan Karadzic, President of the SDS and President of the Republika Srpska, also a para-state entity at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the tape you saw yesterday you recognised the same Radovan Karadzic that you have just mentioned, that he was President of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Karadzic on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also recognised the place where he was speaking, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not able to recognise the place where he was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke of your knowledge of those meetings which would result in the division of Bosnia, your expert opinion is or was formed on documents, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand your question correctly. When I was referring to these alleged partition plans, these were, of course, not documents. These were speculations and this is why I used in my report the word "speculation". I have not seen any document about that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you did not have a single document with their signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen a single document with the signature of either President Tudjman and President Milosevic or the two leaders, Boban and Karadzic saying: "We want to partition Bosnia." I have not seen one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your Honour, all these questions have been answered and asked yesterday, and I see no reason to repeat this again. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): May I continue, Mr President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you might finally push the Trial Chamber to ask the witness not to answer if you insist on repeating questions which have been asked and answered before now. Please, I do not want to be in that position at all. Try and frame your questions properly and go to new issues. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Thank you, your Honours. I accept your suggestion that I should not comment. I just wanted the witness to testify -- to identify the persons she mentioned in her report, and which she spoke of yesterday. You said that there were several newspaper reports. Did you have any Tanjug report, dated 24th/25th February 1992, which reported on a meeting in Graz between the leader of the Serbian Democratic Party, Radovan Karadzic, with envoys of Fanjo Tudjman? Did you also have access to a Tanjug report of 6th May 1992, which carried the report on a meeting between Karadzic and Boban, when they discussed a bilateral agreement on the division of Bosnia and a ceasefire, adding that only the region of Mostar was still under dispute? Did you have in mind a Tanjug report of 11th May 1992 carrying a report by The Washington Post, which comments on this meeting and recalls the Hitler and Stalin pact prior to the Second World War over the division of Poland, pointing out that the meeting was attended by representatives of Tudjman and Milosevic and describing the so-called Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Croatia as "rebel states"? -- "Rogue states" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think the witness should answer that. It is merely a detail not for her to answer. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Closing this part of the cross-examination, could you please answer the following questions: are you aware that at the beginning of 1992 horrific crimes were committed over a large part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you also aware that the regions of Eastern Bosnia and Eastern Herzegovina where UNPROFOR was not present at the time, that these regions were entirely ethnically cleansed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in that period in the first months of the aggression more than 1 million people fled Bosnia-Herzegovina as refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of these waves of mass migrations. I am also aware of the fact that the refugees and displaced people were coming from different nations and nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina 17,000 children were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of the exact numbers, and it appears to be very difficult to give exact numbers even today, as we know from various international organisations, so I cannot confirm this exact number of 17,000 children at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of clarification, I apologise having to repeat what you said yesterday. You confirmed that after April the Yugoslav people's army was a foreign force in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You also confirmed that after its alleged formal withdrawal, the entire logistics, apart of the officer staff remained, and that army enjoyed logistic support all the time. As you have already said that, I would just like to ask you the following: are you aware that the legal armed forces at the beginning of the aggression had an enormous shortage of weapons and logistics essential for defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To clarify, let me just add, as I was speaking on the role of JNA and leaving behind weapons and personnel in Bosnia and giving them to the Bosnian Serbs, that this happened in certain areas in Bosnia but it did not happen in Central Bosnia. It did not happen in the area of Konjic. I should maybe have added this yesterday. As for the question of under-equipment of the Bosnian troops, I think I said this yesterday on several occasions, and of course it was a fact that the Bosnian Army was under-equipped. They had not enough weapons, especially heavy weapons at this early time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the regions controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina were highly dependent on freedom of supply, of food and weaponry across territory controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian Army was dependent in a certain way on the authorities of the para-state of Herceg-Bosna especially. Then it became an issue and when they started quarrelling in mid-1992 and became an even bigger problem after the outbreak of the war between Muslims and Croats in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday on a number of occasions you spoke of the blocade of Sarajevo and the very poor communications between the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you confirm that those communications were very poor also due to lack of resources, logistics and because of repeated attacks on the capital, and that such communication was not only very poor but was completely non-existent at times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is not completely correct. As far as I could see from the documents it was possible from time to time to communicate not with every part -- with other parts of Bosnia, but it really highly depended on the concrete situation and it depended also on the areas. It was not completely isolated.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was not my suggestion either. I just wish you to confirm the fact that the blocade of Sarajevo and constant attacks caused difficulties and sometimes interruptions in communications with other parts of the state, what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Maybe I did not understand your question exactly. I wanted to say from time to time it was blocked but not all the time and not with all the areas.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday you showed us a map showing the military importance of the position of Konjic. Would you please show us again your document number 43?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 43? Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 43 I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the settlements with Serbs as a majority.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. Let me check, please, just for a minute. I apologise. Maybe I gave the wrong number. I think it is this map, so if you could please find it. Maybe you know the number better than me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 44. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): It is 44. I am sorry. I apologise. Can you please tell me where is Borci on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I should put the map where we can see. It is about here, but I have an exact map where we can also see the town of Borci.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This map is interesting, because we can see the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can also see it from this map, but I cannot see it on my screen. Okay. So Borci is here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We cannot see the region to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo is here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The road and the railway from Konjic to Sarajevo cannot be seen, which can be seen on the previous map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we put then maybe -- I don't know how to resolve this problem. 43 ...

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The map that you have on the screen now. Yes, that is the one. Can you please indicate Borci on the map? Can you please tell me where this region was under the control of Serb forces at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What time, please?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After Dayton it was not, but any time before then can you confirm? What I am interested in is the period from May to November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is again a question of these facts which I cannot answer, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think, Mrs Residovic, the Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at 11.45, so that you will continue with your cross-examination. (11.22 am) (Short break)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is still on oath. Now, we will break for lunch at 1, so those doing cross-examination will know how to organise themselves. Yes, you can continue. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. I will need only ten minutes on the outside. Ms Calic, we are back looking at the map that I asked you to show us. Can you please show us Borci. Can you please tell us whether this region was under the control of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have to ask then exactly when, and I would like to repeat that as for the dates, I cannot confirm or not confirm anything.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are confusing me a little. You have asked me to say when and then you say that you cannot confirm or not confirm the dates. I am just asking you about the historical facts. Bearing in mind that you are a doctor of history, you may say that you know or do not know those facts. I will not comment on what you say. Therefore, at the time from the end of April 1992 until the end of 1992, because that is the period that we are interested in in this trial, can you tell us whether Borci was under the control of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you any concrete dates.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Battles are certainly historical events so will you please tell me whether you know that in the region of Borci from June 27th 1992 until the beginning of August 1992 there were significant battles to liberate this region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm or not confirm any of these battles. I am not a fact witness and I am sure there will be fact witnesses who can testify on these events.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wish to underline that these are historical facts, and I understood that the witness is not aware of those historical facts in this region. Can you please indicate Igman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I am not sure when the history could be recorded as a historical fact. It is some years before it settles down. It is too recent to be so sure about it. In most countries I think there is at least 30 years for records to be accepted. She might be a historian, but a historian of a different type, not one about recent battles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Apart from that, so many battles were going on at the same time. She cannot probably pinpoint what particular area was in whose occupation and what fights were going on. So it is a bit difficult for the witness to be more precise in this matter. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I understand, your Honours, and also understand when you give me some indications as to my questioning, but these were political and historical events. The witness has said that she is not just a historian but also a political expert, and she provided more or less a daily political report for her authorities so that they might be guided in taking political decisions, but anyway it is not my place to comment on that, so I will continue with my questions. Can you show us on the map you have offered as a document Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I have got a map of Mount Igman too. I show this map. Yes, Mount Igman. No, not Mount Igman. Mount Igman is about here. Where is Sarajevo? Yes, about here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that from the industry of Sarajevo in the direction of Konjic there are many mountains: the mountains of Igman, Bjelasnica and Treskavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that throughout this period Sarajevo was besieged and continually exposed to attack by Serbian forces who besieged it, in this period from May until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And under constant military attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that as of June, as early as June 1992, and especially as of the end of July, heavy fighting erupted and attempts were made by Bosnian defensive forces to lift the blockade of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these attempts were made. I mentioned them yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that in that period a major operation known as "South 92" was organised in August 1992 and that that battle went on for several months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only have two or three more questions linked to your knowledge regarding the large number of refugees that arrived in Konjic. You said that there were 8,000 of them, but you allowed the possibility that other documents may speak of a larger number too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I rely on the figures given by the UNHCR, which I believe is a reliable source. I have not seen any other figures, and I cannot confirm that there was a bigger numbers, but I rely here on the UNHCR report.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For a town with 13,000 inhabitants, would you agree that 8,000 is a very large number of refugees arriving to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I must maybe also add that 80,000, the figure given by the UNHCR, meant all the refugees coming in until now, so I do not know exactly which months in 1992, how many refugees arrived from other areas. These persons might also have come later on during the war, as many people often left Konjic, as you know. 10,000 Croats also left the municipality of Konjic, 6,000 Serbs and 10 thousand Croats left and 8,000 displaced persons were coming in during the war so I do not know exactly now in which months how many left and came in.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of members of all nationalities left Konjic during the war operations, including Bosnians and refugees came in, but I am asking: given the constant hostilities and the large number of refugees coming in after atrocious personal experiences, can you confirm that the responsible authorities of Konjic municipality, which were insufficiently prepared for the war, had vast difficulties in dealing with the basic questions of the survival of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree on this, but I would also like to add that this was not only the case in Konjic. This was the case in many, many municipalities in Bosnia. It was also the case in municipalities where the Serbs had the majority. There were also Serb displaced persons coming there. Also these municipalities had, of course, big problems. I just would like to emphasis this was an overall phenomenon. It did not happen openly in Konjic, but, in fact, it created big problems.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you about the municipality of Konjic, and probably you will have occasion to express your expert opinion regarding other matters. Can you agree with me that this problem was much greater in the towns under siege and which were exposed to constant hostile activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towns which were under siege, I do not know if to towns under siege displaced persons could come in in big numbers. Maybe I did not get your question correctly. Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The difficulties confronting the local authorities in towns that were exposed to constant attacks were far greater than those in which there were no such attacks on a daily basis. You mentioned others, for instance, Prijedor -- there were no hostile activities in town -- or maybe Bihac, Gorazde. These were towns where the war was on constantly. Were difficulties in towns exposed to constant attack much greater than those in other places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, in areas where there was heavy fighting the problems were bigger than in areas where there was no heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My last question for you, Ms Calic, is: were the difficulties in terms of survival in the territory of the municipality of Konjic multi-fold and did they require enormous effort on the part of each individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am convinced that in each municipality, in each village, in each town where there was heavy fighting, people of whatever nationality did suffer very hardly, and I believe it was really a big problem for all people exposed to fighting and destruction, expulsion, war crimes. It was a big problem.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I asked the witness to show me this morning the documents on the basis of which she compiled her own document number 50. If the witness can provide access to that source material, I will ask you, if necessary, to allow me to ask more questions on the basis of that document. Will I be permitted to do that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually it depends on what earlier questions you have asked. If there are new questions not connected with whatever has been asked, it might be relevant, but aside from that, it might not be necessary. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes. Thank you. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Exhibit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are we awaiting other cross-examinations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I thought it was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then I will wait, your Honour. As to these documents, your Honour, I just want to inform you they are being copied and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not able to find an index. Is there an index?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: There is an index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was just wondering where it is. Point out the page where the index is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you not have it in your hand now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have been trying to find out the index. I have not been able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In the beginning of the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Karabdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, please let us go on with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You have any cross-examination? MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): I would like to cross-examine the witness and I would like the Chamber to allow me to move to the lectern, so that I could be better heard, and I would be closer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You can do so. You can move to the centre. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Ms Calic, my name is Salih Karabdic, counsel from Sarajevo, and defence counsel for Hazim Delic. I will ask you several questions relating to your expert report and your testimony given today. I will not repeat the questions asked by my learned colleague, Ms Residovic, but I will need to ask questions from similar areas but from a different aspect. Ms Calic, is Bosnia-Herzegovina in the present day borders and the borders from 1942 until the outbreak of the war -- was Bosnia occupied by Austro-Hungary in the period between 1878 until 1918?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Bosnia was under Austro-Hungarian administration until 1908 and it came under Austro-Hungarian occupation, and then after the end of the First World War it became part of the first Yugoslav state, the so-called state of the Serbs, the Croats and the Slovenes, which in 1929 became the name Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Throughout this period of the Austro-Hungarian rule did it have its own bodies, its own Governor and government and all institutions as a separate entity within Austro-Hungary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a separate administrative unit. It was, of course, not a state in the modern sense but it was a unit of administration administered by Austrian and Hungarian administration.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Was this area defined as a corpus separatum, that is a separate body, and in my view that is a separate body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was kind of separate from the rest of Austro-Hungary, but still it was under administration and later on occupation. It was occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Were elections held in this area, in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was any representative body ever established throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the modern sense of the word. There were elections, of course, at this time. The first multi-party elections were held in the Yugoslavia time and in the first Yugoslav state Bosnia did not exist in administrative borders or republican borders. It was just a part of a common Yugoslav state.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: My question was: during the Austro-Hungarian period was a representative body ever formed, established, during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a separate unit. It was a separate territory, but still under the rule of Austro-Hungary. Many decisions were taken actually by the Austro-Hungarian emperors, yes, but it was separate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: The laws that were adopted by Austro-Hungary for some areas were not automatically extended to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. There were laws for different parts of the big empire of Austro-Hungary. They were laws differently in different parts of this empire.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: When the Yugoslavia was established, is it correct that within Yugoslavia up until 1927 or 1929, maybe 1926 -- I may not have the year correctly -- was Bosnia a separate territorial entity within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so, because at that time Yugoslavia was divided up in administrative units and later on in the so-called banovina, and you cannot compare. Yugoslavia was more or less a centralised state, in first Yugoslavia in the inter-war period. It was only after the Second World War that Bosnia became one of six republics within a federal state, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. May I maybe also say that it may not be so relevant for our case, and we should recognise, acknowledge, that Bosnia as a state was recognised internationally in 1992, and maybe it helps us to understand the history and the legal status of this republic, and going back to history may not help us too much in this case. I emphasised many times Bosnia in 1992 became an independent, sovereign republic.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I agree with you on that point, but in the circumstances of today or at least since 1992 we cannot fully understand unless we also look at the whole process and history, but I will limit myself as much as I can and ask as few questions from that area as I can. In your report you rely on historical facts, and I need to ask you for some clarifications of these historical facts. In 1878, after the Congress of Berlin, when Turkey ceded its control and administration of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Austro-Hungary, was Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, when it was turned over to Austro-Hungary -- was that Bosnia-Herzegovina within the Turkish empire also a separate administrative unit, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: And was it turned over to Austro-Hungary with the exception of the Sandzak area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the borders of this separate administrative unit of Bosnia-Herzegovina towards Austro-Hungary already established through the Peace of Karlovci, which had taken place more than a century before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less, yes. I think I answered this question already yesterday but of course I can answer it again.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question here. Is the area that is defined as Herzegovina today -- was this area part of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the period of Austro-Hungarian rule and the Turkish period; in other words was it part of this administrative unit, that unit that was administrated by those two states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Was this area of Herzegovina part of the medieval state of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the very centre of the creation of the Bosnian state, the medieval Bosnian state.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Would you then please clarify for me what historical causes you quote in your report when you say that Croats are basing their territorial claims on historical reasons when they ask to include this part of Herzegovina to the Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately history has been used on many occasions to justify territorial aspirations and to justify political aims, and this is also why, being a historian, I do not like to use history too much in these contexts. It depends which century you go back to. If we start and say, well, in the Middle Ages this territory was maybe Bosnian but 200 years ago, 500 years ago, there might have been another people ruling, another empire ruling in this area, so the population structure changed throughout the centuries, and this gave occasion to the Croats to lay claim on this territory. Many parts of Herzegovina are settled dominantly by Croats, and we can, of course -- I do not argue whether or not historically it is justified. I just wanted to point out that the Croats -- and the Croatians -- and the Croats, they do so. They do lay claim on this territory, even though it was historically part of the Bosnian state, of a medieval state, but history may change many things and there are so many centuries between -- 5, 6, 7 centuries between these events and even more. 1,000 years of history, let me say.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Then I am not sure if I had not misunderstood your explanation. That means that in the historical facts and in the historical development there is no basis for such tendency and such claims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Being a historian, I think I am competent enough to say that we should not argue with history. It will bring us in big difficulties. You see the Serbian medieval kingdom was very big. If we argue there is a continuity of the Serb medieval state until now, then it would even include Bulgaria. Where would we go if I say: look, Germany in the middle ages how big it is? Of course we cannot argue like this. Being a historian myself, I am of the opinion here we are dealing with political questions. We are in the middle of the 20th century and we are exactly now here in the 1990s. So I do not argue on the basis of these arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the basis of relevance I want to object to this line of questioning going on for such a long time. As Dr Calic herself has pointed out, it is not relevant for this case what happened far back in the centuries, and I think it is not relevant at all for trying these four accused persons for their crimes in Celebici camp to have this per se very interesting history lesson. So I would ask the court to remind Mr Karabdic to confine himself to things relevant to this case and do not take the time of this trial to give us this long history lesson. Thank you very much. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I was only looking for clarification of the report submitted by this expert witness and these historical reasons are quoted there. They are connected with the explanation of the events in that area that are linked to this case. So it is my view that I can ask for clarifications, and I do not agree with this kind of objection on the part of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask whatever clarifications you want, if the witness is able to give them. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): I do not insist that the witness provide clarifications. If she can, that is fine. If I just try to elucidate a point. If the witness is unable to do that, that is fine with me. Do you know that in Bosnia-Herzegovina there exists a number of Jews and that been there for over 500 years, the Jews that came there and were received there in Bosnia after they were expelled from the Catholic Spain. Do you know that throughout that time they lived freely, and they worked freely, and they had freedom of religion. They even kept their language, Spanish, and a very important document from their history while they lived in Spain was preserved. It is called Hagada. Are you familiar with all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with that. I have seen many documents. I have seen also the fabulous exhibition in Sarajevo before the war exactly on the Jews. I have read numbers of books on this but again I cannot see exactly how this very interesting historical fact fits into this context.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I would just like to add to what you have already given as a response to my colleague just as another proof that in Bosnia the principle of tolerance, the ethnic and religious tolerance, has always been a long -- that it is of long-term tradition in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is indeed a long-term tradition of tolerance in this country.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in Bosnia the rule that was around "cuius regio eius religio" ruled in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: In that light the population, the ethnic group that is called Bosnians or Muslims, did they voluntarily accept Islam during the Ottoman rule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appears that part of the population did voluntarily and parts of the population were also forced, because the Turks or the Ottomans did also recruit. Among non-Turks, among the Slavic people, and these often young men were recruited by force. Of course, they were also too young to decide, and then became Muslims. They were often taken away from their homes, but a part of the populations did it voluntarily, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Those who accepted Islam as their religion, did these people preserve -- did the people who accepted Islam as their own religion preserve their ethnic origins, their ethnic character? Did they stay the same nation or did they keep their culture, their traditions by adopting the Muslim religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they kept parts of their culture, but they adapted also new elements of culture, of Islamic culture. Maybe I cannot understand your question very well but of course they remained in the tradition of what they were before.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they preserve their separate alphabet, a cyrillic form called Bosancica, and did they use it throughout the Ottoman rule and even later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That people, did it have its own literature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did it have a developed oral literature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Were the products of that literature well-known to the world, Hasanaginica and Merima, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this people has a rich tradition of literature.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me whether it is correct that the language spoken in Bosnia specifically in Eastern Herzegovina served as a basis for the literary language that Serbs took over through Vuk Karadzic as well as the Croats through Ljudevit Gai?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will have to now move a little -- I will not take long -- away from the region of Bosnia. Are you aware that throughout this region of, let me call it former Yugoslavia, or rather Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Macedonia, that during the Turkish administration, churches, monasteries were preserved, even though that administration lasted for more than 500 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is that evidence of religious tolerance that ruled in that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Are you aware too that in Serbia, in Belgrade and in other places there were large communities of people of Islamic faith, of Slavic origin, and do you know that all of them were expelled or forced to convert to Christianity when the Serbian state was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a big part of them were expelled, and yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: What happened to the rest, those who were not expelled? Were they Christianed or not? Did they convert or not by force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most had to convert by force, but this is again history.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I just wish to explain that this is a programme, this is the consequence of a programme. This is the same principle that I mentioned a moment ago. Serbia implemented this principle in relation to the Slavs, even Serbs, just because they were of a different faith. Please, do you know that throughout this region of Serbia there was a large number of mosques, medresas, cemeteries and that with the exception of one or two, that all this has been destroyed and ruined to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of these buildings have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: They do not exist today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like again to object, if you please. We have now been having this historical background for something like half an hour, and as far as I can understand, Mr Karabdic has not so far reached the point of cross-examination. There is nothing in this questioning -- anything of what Dr Calic has said pertaining to the background. So I cannot see that this is a cross-examination. We are going through a new historical area not even touched upon by the witness now cross-examined, and I think you have to guide the defence lawyer to keep within the parameters of the cross-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I have never understood it to be so limited to what you want to hear. Cross-examination can be wide. As long as he wants his targets, he might even lead her into areas she might show her ignorance. I do not think there is anything wrong with it. It depends on what he is looking for. It is his case. Let him make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So far, your Honour, I do not know what he is looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You may not know. Finally you will see what he is looking for. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours, for allowing me to continue. I will end soon. I just wish to show that in this area too the same policy was implemented which was implemented before. I have just one more question in this area. You said that you took your doctoral thesis on Serbia and its development during the last century and the beginning of the 20th century. Are you aware that after the Balkan Wars terrible crimes were committed and a large number of civilians were killed, to such an extent by the Serbian army and the Serbs that the international community was concerned about it and that it set up a Commission, which was to investigate this, and that that Commission did not complete its work merely because of the outbreak of the First World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the findings of the Carnegie Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask some questions about Konjic. You mentioned that the road M17 passes through Konjic, which is the main link, not just the main one but the only one between Sarajevo and the sea, and the coast; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The road linking Sarajevo running through Konjic to the coast is indeed a very important communication line.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is that the only link with the coast, especially now during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I show this other map, my document number 44? Of course Bosnia had also other roads running from Sarajevo down here and you could, of course, reach also by other ways the coast, but during this time this area was under Serb control. Sarajevo was mainly linked through this road with the coast.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: In your report in connection with this road and the region of Konjic you mentioned Stolac-Nevesinja-Kalinovik-Sarajevo and Dubrovnik-Gacko-Foca. Do those roads cross the region of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did explain, I think, very clearly yesterday that these roads are not running through the municipality of Konjic, but they belong to the territory of Herzegovina and in this broader context these communication lines became also very important, even if they do not run exactly through the municipality of Konjic, but I have also prepared a map to show this. They were near to Konjic and they were of a big also importance for reaching the eastern part of this country. I think I did explain this yesterday. I showed also this map.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Those other roads were under the control of the Serbs and the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in this court you mentioned that Serb settlements were along this main road, M17. Are you aware that even before the war and at the beginning of the war they put up barricades on that road preventing free passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read about this in several witness's reports, but I cannot personally confirm these reports. I read about it.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If what you read is true, does every authority, including the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, have the right to prevent such blockage of passage and disturbance of traffic, particularly when an important road is involved, one that is essential for supply along which food supplies and other supplies come in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a clear interest of controlling these areas. I am not in a position to say whether it was right or legal. I can state objectively it was a fact; it was important. It was an interest to control these areas, especially in the conditions of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not insisting too much on this, but could you perhaps on the basis of the reports that you mentioned tell us when or whether you can see from those reports when the shelling of Konjic started from the air, air raids and shelling of Konjic? Can you see that from the reports that you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I read reports on it. I read witness's statements, but I cannot confirm whether or not it is true. It is up to this court to bring the facts together and to decide whether or not the witnesses are credible. I cannot testify on this.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I asked about the reports, but very well. Please, did the municipality of Konjic in 1990, when the elections were held -- did it elect its municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did that Assembly elect its Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did the Assembly have a President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Therefore, did that body, that is the municipal authorities, were they functioning? Were they legally elected, and did they function up to the war and after, and during the war -- up to the war? I will ask separately for the period of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently it ceased to function because the Serb representatives who were also elected withdrew from these bodies, and so apparently they did not function any more from March onwards. According to the elections of 1990 the Serbs were not represented any more.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but, please, were the elections carried out in the municipality and deputies elected, and did the majority of those deputies require a quorum, and for the functioning of the Assembly were they always there in the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I read contradictory reports.
