I read reports from the Serb side saying there were reprisals and they were not allowed to participate any more, and I read reports from other witnesses saying that the Serbs were withdrawing voluntarily, and they did simply not want to participate any more in these bodies. So I really cannot say whether or not they withdraw voluntarily or whether they were forced to. I just say that apparently these bodies from March onwards did not function any more in the way they were functioning before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Please, you gave the composition of that Assembly and after the withdrawal of those deputies, those Serbs, was there a sufficient number of deputies for the Assembly to function according to the law, to pass decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It brings me back to the same answer. The Serbs contested this fact. They contested the legitimacy of this Assembly, as they did contest the legitimacy of the republican Assembly. It is not up to me to decide whether they were right or not. I just wanted to explain this was the view of the Serbs, and, of course, the remaining members of this Assembly had a different view on this. They continued to believe that this was a legitimate body, even though the elected representative of the Serbs did not participate any more in these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I want to ask a question. Were they elected by nationality for spaces or from a joint elected group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were elected jointly but most parties were defined ethnically or they had a clear basis towards one nationality, although, in fact, all Serbs or most Serbs voted the Serb SDS and most Muslims voted then the SDA and so on. There were very few parties who were constituted on a multi-national level. Nobody did say so openly, but, in fact, this was the case, and the name of the SDS is also Serb Democratic Party. It says "Serb Democratic Party". But there was the idea also coming from the tradition of Bosnia before the war that all people should be represented in these bodies, and after the first multi-party elections in 1990 the main officials of Bosnia stick to this principle. They were convinced that they should go on working together and having represented all three constitutive people of Bosnia in the highest body, beyond the republican level, beyond the municipal level, but then as the conflicts erupted and tensions were growing and the Serbs were just contesting the Muslims and the Croats were acting legally, this kind of compromise or this kind of power sharing did not function any more. It did not function on the republican level and it did not function on the municipal level. Again I just tried to explain the different views.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I did not ask you for views. I asked you regarding the fact. What was the necessary quorum? Do you know what quorum is necessary for a meeting to be held and for the Municipal Assembly to function, and whether such a quorum existed even after the withdrawal of the Serbs? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what exact number the quorum was. I know that the Serbs contested the legitimacy of acting without them. They have been elected to participate in the work of these bodies, and after their withdrawal they were not represented any more, and it was not the idea of power-sharing from before the war and from also 1990 and onwards to exclude one of the nations from important decisions. Again I cannot say whether they withdrew voluntarily or whether they were forced to do so, but they did, and after that they contested the legitimacy of making decisions on the basis that they were not present any more.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: We know all the reasons that they gave, but did the constitution, the statute of the municipality, -- was there any stipulation except a stipulation that there must be a certain quorum for a body to function? The regulations that existed during the time of Yugoslavia -- was there any such provision in the law? If the majority of deputies are present, the Assembly was a quorum and it can function. They all represent the people and thereby they represent that particular territory, or what was known then as a socio-political community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I tried to explain earlier this morning that usually if democratically elected bodies ceased to function because maybe one party withdraws, then you should have new elections, and you have to elect a new body that functions, but this was, of course, impossible under these circumstances. I think we cannot argue with the legalistic way the Serbs were contesting this, claiming that they were forced to expel, and there was repression and reprisals. I cannot say whether it is true. It is what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just wanted you to explain to me whether there were any regulations in the rules of procedure, in the statute or the constitution which required some other kind of qualified majority except for a simple majority. Did any such regulations envisage a particular structure of that majority? Were there any such regulations or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you are referring. Maybe I cannot -- I'm not capable of understanding you, but I will try. Maybe you can explain it again to me. I was saying before that the Serbs claimed they were forced to withdraw from these bodies, and therefore they said there is no legal, legitimate basis any more for these bodies making decisions, and I myself cannot tell you whether or not they were right or they were not right. Maybe they were not right, but maybe -- I can't tell you. I am just trying to explain that there were different views. One saying: "Even if you withdraw, we can make legitimate decisions". This is one view. The other view is: "If you withdraw, you cannot make any decisions; you cannot make decisions on our behalf." This is my understanding of the situation. Usually if you reach such a blocade of views, you should try to find a way out and you should try to find a compromise. In democratic countries you then have new elections. This was not possible under these circumstances and in this time.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I asked you, as you are an expert witness on the political and historical conditions and relationships in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the Konjic region -- I just asked whether there was any constitutional or legal provision according to which, if a certain majority, a certain number, a quorum of deputies come to a session, preventing it from meeting, if a certain number of deputies are absent and have not come. As far as I know, every representative body has regulations and provisions governing its work, and enabling it to pass decisions if a certain number of deputies are present, regardless of the fact that the others are not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe you should take into consideration the whole range of legal provisions and the idea of this, as I was pointing out before, to have represented all constituent nations, and, from the understanding of the Bosnian, as you were saying, also in view of this long tradition of tolerance -- and there was also a tradition of power-sharing -- it was regulated like this that all constituent nations should be represented in an appropriate way in the decision-making bodies. We heard yesterday your colleague told us correctly that after the Bosnian State Presidency broke up and the SDS representatives walked out, they were replaced by other Serbs. So we should see the whole range of the original idea, of what was behind the idea of sharing power in an ethnically mixed surrounding. We should bear this in mind. It was also for historical reasons very important to stick to this principle of power-sharing, especially in very critical moments, when power was contested and when nearly everything over this country was contested. I really think there were different views on this.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether regulations, laws, the constitution -- it is another matter if individual parties came to an agreement to share power or to act together. There are always coalitions. So in Bosnia too such coalitions could have existed but it does not mean if one coalition partner is absent, if he withdraws, that then the whole system collapses, and that decisions of such an assembly are invalid, and that such an assembly cannot function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if this is again a legal question which I am not capable of understanding or of answering in an appropriate way, but usually let us say in democratic countries if the elected members of an Assembly or of a body are not able to come in agreement on important things and one side decides not to participate any more, then you should elect new and with new persons you then may come to an agreement. This is the idea of then having new elections and newly- elected bodies, and I cannot see why this is not a good way of solving such blockades of political organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we have reached the end of the road for this session. We are still not out of the woods. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, if I may, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. The witness is still on her oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Miss Calic, may I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are still cross-examining or have you concluded? You are still continuing your cross-examination? MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): With your permission, I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): I apologise to the judge. Apologies to your Honours. This is an awkward, cumbersome binder. So indulge me, please. Ms Calic, in your report you state that in March 1992 the administrative bodies and the authorities of the Konjic municipality ceased to function. That should be a fact. Since you stated that you were not witness to these events, that you were not an eye witness there, would you please tell me on what basis did you state that in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I drew this conclusion on the basis of different documents, on the basis of the fact that there were established crisis staffs and on the basis of witness statements telling that -- telling me about the withdrawal of the Serbs from these bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Did the members of the SDS resign their memberships or just stay away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed away. Of course, I don't know exactly because there are contradictory reports on this. I read reports saying there was also force. They were not allowed any more to participate. So I do not personally know how exactly this happened. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Do you know that after the withdrawal of Serbs from the Assembly of the Konjic municipality, that is the members of the SDS, that there were Serbs who were in this assembly, who were properly elected from this territory, who remained in this body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know what the exact ethnic composition of the remaining body was. I have no documents about that, no documentation. I have not seen one single document on this.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: In your report it is stated that the Konjic municipality had 60 representatives; is that correct and that out of this 60 -- out of this 40 -- no, out of this 60 there were only 9 were from the SDS party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: And if I understood you properly, you would like to make us believe that if out of 60 representatives 9 representatives leave, the Assembly becomes non-legal or illegitimate, and that it cannot go on functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do actually not have an opinion whether or not this was lawful or unlawful. I instead have an opinion on the fact that it was a tradition and also a legal tradition in Bosnia that power should be shared according to the national composition, and to support this view I brought a document. This is the report of the Election Commission from 1991. It is more precisely the report on the election results of 1990, and there is an interesting last part in which the election results and the members elected are compared with the ethnic composition of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are still translating this and then we will hand it over. This Election Commission refers to several constitution Articles and laws, and it evidently was the case that the nationalities should not be over or under-represented more or less than 15 per cent of their share of population. So this is just to show you that it was obviously a common view and a shared view, also from a legal point of view that people should be represented in the elected bodies according to their ethnic representation, according to their population share. I have not to decide whether or not this is lawful or unlawful. It is published in the Official Gazette, 19th December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: You are answering a question that I did not ask, but that is a completely separate issue of the elections, but that would depart from what we are trying to clarify here, but in the election law there was a provision where it is stated that the election results should not deviate from the ethnic position of the population of plus/minus 15 percentage points. That is a general provision which only referred to the elections, whereas I asked you -- my question is about the functioning of the Assembly and its legality. Any Assembly is legal and legitimate if it has a quorum, is that not so, if the quorum exists? Was there any regulation that these nine members of the SDS had to be present at sessions, that without them no decisions should be taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I am not a lawyer. I cannot say whether or not this was lawful or unlawful. I am just explaining that the Serbs, after their withdrawal, were considering that it was unlawful. I am just explaining this was one view. There might be another view saying that it was lawful, but it is not up to me to decide about this question. It is a legal question. I am not a lawyer. I cannot answer you this question.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: In other words, you are saying that in your report you stated the Serbian position, because it was their view that by their departure the Assembly ceased to function, the Assembly of the municipality of Konjic. You did not mention the other opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will submit this document by the Election Commission of Bosnia, which states that the elected members of the Assembly should also reflect the ethnic composition of the population and deviation should not be bigger than plus/minus 15 per cent. This is not my personal view. This is what the Election Commission stated referring to Serbian laws. This will be translated and then submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I do not want to repeat myself. That is as a result of the elections, but for the functioning of the Assembly itself, that has not been stipulated. However, I want to continue. Is the Municipal Assembly of Konjic -- did it also have an Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had an Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Was this Executive Council -- was that still existing, and in your opinion it seemed to have also ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood from the documents which I have seen that according to what was the use in Bosnia before the war, after the elections of 1990 the Executive Council of Konjic included members of different nations, parties, nationalities. I also understood from the documents then in March 1992 the Serb representatives left also this council. So this council maybe existed but the Serbs were not represented any more. Again it comes back to the same question, which I cannot answer, whether or not this was legal or illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Executive Council is a body that implements the decisions of the Municipal Assembly; in other words it is an executive body, it is a working body, and it can continue to work based on the directions on the part of the Assembly. So it is not a representational body. It should be unaffected by whether all the population segments were represented in it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I wanted to show is that the political and administrative structures started to disintegrate from March 1992 onwards at the latest, maybe even earlier. They started to disintegrate in ethnic components. This is what I wanted to show. I did, of course, not intend to make any legal comments on this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Still I can agree with you that certain steps and individual steps or maybe the steps that one large party had done could have led towards this disintegration. However, Bosnia did not disintegrate. It survived. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia as a state did survive, but unfortunately it is partitioned in two among a common roof of state. Ethnic separation is a fact in today's Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: My question was not what is the situation today but Bosnia has survived and it has been recognised. It is a different matter of its internal organisation and structure right now. In the same way the Konjic municipality also survived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But in a completely different ethnic shape.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I am speaking about the Konjic municipality as authority and as a territory. As authority, it survived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask another question. In your report you mentioned a provision from the HB constitution, Article 272, on the War Presidency of the municipality. Pursuant to this Article was the main task of the Presidency of the municipality in the time of war or threat of war to carry out the functions of the Municipal Assembly, if it is unable to meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, which supports in a way my view the Assembly did not work any more, otherwise the formation of a War Presidency would have been illegal, is it not.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the immediate danger or threat was proclaimed and that the conditions in the Konjic municipality were such that the Municipal Assembly could not meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is it then correct to say that certain functions of the Municipal Assembly were taken over by the War Presidency pursuant to the law and the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you wish, I can show you something. We had addressed the issue of the law of the all people's defence, and from it it was -- it came in force on the day when it was published in the Official Gazette, which was 20th May 1992. This is in reference to Article 42, which speaks to the -- addresses the issue of the War Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated here regarding Territorial Defence -- you said that it is established in the local communes, in companies, that units are formed and they have their own weapons, which they use and which they acquire because -- it comes from the budgets of the companies and the municipalities and such; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Yugoslav Army took away all these weapons from the Territorial Defence, even though the republic, the local communes, municipalities and different companies had provided it through their own means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that JNA took away a bigger part of these weapons from the territory of Bosnia, certain municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you know what municipalities those were where the weapons were taken away, and were the weapons taken away in municipalities where Croats and Muslims were in the majority and were they left where the Serbs were in the majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course the attempt was made to transfer all the weapons from Muslim and Croat majority areas to areas settled predominantly by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question in reference to Konjic. In your report you said that the JNA and that the Serbian side -- but mostly the JNA -- that they were weakened in this region by the decision of the rump Presidency of the then Yugoslavia regarding the pull-out of the army from Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correctly stated in your report? Is that how it was stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood from the document which I also included in this binder that the local JNA commanders were aware of the fact that they were in a difficult position keeping the JNA in areas where Muslims and Croats had already built up their armed forces, and they felt surrounded. This was, of course, different in areas where the Serbs were in the majority but in the specific Central Bosnian area my impression was that they were trying to pull out.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you think and do the facts show that in that period the JNA was occupied by deploying in Eastern Bosnia and could not spare the necessary forces for Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression was that Central Bosnia was at this moment of minor importance for the JNA and they had concentrated their forces in other areas of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move to another area of questioning. This would conclude my questioning on Konjic, but I would like to continue with questions of more general nature. In your report you state that not any of the republics within Yugoslavia was inhabited by a single nation. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: And by saying this you obviously consider it to be something extraordinary or strange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I don't. I consider it natural for this area, for the whole area of -- south-eastern area -- it is a very common fact that republics comprise several nations and nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Does this apply only to the area of Eastern Europe or worldwide? Let us take, for instance, the former USSR. There are Russians in all the republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: And in some up to 40 per cent, but when the USSR was disintegrating, they became the citizens of these new republics, new republics and states which withdrew from the union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in some republics they were fighting wars or in some areas about this question. It was indeed similar to the disintegration of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I say that this cannot compare -- rather, do you consider that this can be compared with what happened in the area of the former Yugoslavia? The largest conflict occurred over something else. That is in the Tzecens, where an autonomous republic within the Russian confederation sought independence. Conflict did not erupt between Russians and the local population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not introduce this example myself. I think what we can compare is there were also problems concerning the question of succession, and succession was a big problem in Yugoslavia and it still remains a big problem. Not all questions concerning succession could be settled as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: The questions of succession and other disputed issues among civilised peoples are resolved in appropriate ways and within appropriate institutions, but in Yugoslavia there was a general blood-bath; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia there was at this time, at the time when Yugoslavia fell apart, no agreement on how the question of succession should be settled, and it appears to me until now not all these questions could be settled, even after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Was the decision of the Badinter Commission a step or position that was important for succession? Did that decision confirm the right of each republic to decide whether it will become independent or will join with another republic, and this right was recognised after it was established that Yugoslavia was disintegrating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I ask for indulgence, your Honour, until I put some order in my papers. You mentioned three national parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party wanted something for the Serbian people, and that is why it called itself the Serbian Democratic Party. The Croatian Democratic Alliance wanted something for the Croatian people, and it called itself for that reason the Croatian Democratic Alliance, and its membership is limited to Croats and Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this is not correct, because, if I remember correctly, there was a Bosnian law saying that the parties are not allowed to exclude according to nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, I agree that such a regulation existed, but it is a fact that in their programmes and their activities they sought things only for the Serbian or the Croatian people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would see it, of course, differently, but they were national-oriented.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Please, as far as the Party of Democratic Action is concerned, is it correct that in its programme it laid down that all that it is asking for the Muslims, that it recognises the same to other citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can then the SDA be treated as a party with an exclusive national programme, or is it a party with a programme for a Bosnia of equal citizens of all ethnic groups and religions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It claimed to be a party that -- it claims to be a party for all citizens and for all nations of Bosnia, at least at the beginning of the multi-party system in Bosnia, but one should also see that many Croats and many Serbs simply did not trust in this programme. They did not trust what was on paper and they therefore did not take into consideration to vote for this party. Also a minor part of Croats and Serbs maybe voted for the SDA. This explains maybe also why they did not get more votes or significantly more votes than the share of the Muslim population was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is it true that a considerable number of Muslims did not vote for the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were probably Muslims who did not vote for the SDA, as there were Croats and Serbs who did not vote for HDZ and for SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the Assembly was formed and began to function, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the elections of 1990 -- no, I apologise. Let me start again. At the 1990 elections was the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina elected, and how many chambers did it have? You said it was bicameral. Thank you. Did all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina vote for that Assembly? There were no separate polling stations or separate lists based on ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if I understood the question. The lists were not according to nationality. No, I think I understood. There were no lists according to nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Was voting on the basis of nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: At those elections was the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina elected by direct ballot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have witnesses here present that at those elections in 1990 the Presidency was elected at direct elections, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you deny that fact, then that is something else, if you claim that was not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I maybe did not get your question correctly. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: At the 1990 elections directly by the voters, by direct ballot, was the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina elected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did all the citizens vote for that Presidency; I mean all the citizens who voted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who had the right to vote or who voted?

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: No, no. I am asking -- very well. Let me make myself clearer. The composition of the Presidency, what was the composition of the Presidency? Do you know the composition of the Presidency by ethnic origin that was elected in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were seven members, 3:2:2.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there were two Muslims, two Croats, two Serbs and one Yugoslav. Please, did all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina vote for the Serbs, for the Croats, or, rather, did they have the right to vote for a Muslim, a Croat, a Serb and others, or did only -- did the Muslims elect the Muslim, the Serbs the Serb and the Croats the Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no lists according to nationality. The votes were also secret. They were secret elections.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I want an explanation, please. The candidates were elected an a national basis during the elections. Of the candidates for the Presidency, did all the citizens vote on that? Did I as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina vote or somebody else both for the Serbian candidate and the Croatian candidate, or did I have the right only to vote for the Muslim candidate? That is my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were equal votes. You have had, of course, not more than your own vote. I think also this can be clarified by the document which is being translated, because exactly these problems are in here, and the composition ... maybe we should wait until we get this document.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you. I am sorry. Do you claim that I, as a Muslim, could vote only for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I do not claim this. I claim that elections were secret and each person who had the right to vote of course could vote for the person of whatever nationality he or she wanted. A Serb could vote for a Muslim candidate and a Muslim could vote for a Serb candidate or Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. This means that the whole of Bosnia participated in the election of that Presidency regardless of the ethnic background of the voters; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, when the Assembly elected at those elections and the Presidency started to function, a government was formed. You said that two disputed issues arose, the question of the independence of Bosnia and the question of its constitutional set-up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to ask, please, the leadership at the time, the state leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it in favour of Bosnia being proclaimed an independent country? Did it immediately want the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was that its aim and programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not at the beginning. It was at the beginning to find a compromise between the two opposing views of the Slovenes and Croats, on the one side, who were in favour of independence, and of the Serbs, on the other side, who wanted to preserve Yugoslavia. They had an intermediate position at the beginning. The Bosnian government had an intermediate position at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Please, did the Presidency and government of Bosnia try to preserve Yugoslavia? Did it seek to preserve Yugoslavia within its borders and to avoid disintegration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they made a proposal which made also changes with regard to the constitution, so it was not exactly the same Yugoslavia that had existed before.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: The initiator of that proposal, who was the initiator? Was it the state leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina or did it -- was it forced to make such proposals because of the events in Slovenia and Croatia and Serbia so as to find a compromise solution which everyone could accept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am again not sure if I understand your question but as far as I understand it, it was a reaction to what was happening and the dissolution of Yugoslavia was already on its way. So it has to be understood in the context of the dissolution of Yugoslavia. It was a proposal made after Croatia and Slovenia had made their proposals and after Serbia had made its proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the proposal of Gligorov Izetbegovic on the preservation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was rejected by the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment please. Can I conclude from this or can it be concluded from your statement that the question of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina arose only after the events in Serbia, Slovenia and Croatia and after the inability to find -- to reach a compromise; in other words, that the question of independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina was set in motion by events outside it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It happened in the context of the disintegration of Yugoslavia as a state and it came maybe too late for being an acceptable compromise for all the sides because the Slovene and Croat governments had already decided to leave the country, so maybe it was too late for success for this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: In any event, I agree with you that perhaps it was too late, but in any event it was a step, an attempt to preserve Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, the question of the Resolution on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed on 14th November 1991. I don't quite understand. You used different terms. Maybe it is due to the interpretation or my own misunderstanding. Do you consider by that act did Bosnia proclaim itself to be independent, or did it just confirm its sovereign right to decide its future destiny itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not precisely a declaration on sovereignty, but it stated as well that Yugoslavia -- Bosnia did not intend to stay in a Yugoslavia in which Croatia and Slovenia did not participate at the same time. So we can also understand this declaration of sovereignty as a first step forwards independence regarding the fact that Slovenia and Croatia had already declared their independence from Yugoslavia and this declaration of sovereignty was made months later in October 1991, but formally it was a declaration on sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. I want to ask a question. It is not really related to what counsel is asking from you. The referendum in Bosnia was held on 29th February and 1st March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When was the formal declaration of independence issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And by whom was it issued, now being an independent state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have several steps. We have the first step towards independence, which was this declaration of sovereignty in October 1991. Then we have on 20th December 1992 -- 1991 we have the letter requesting independence, and this letter was sent by the President Izetbegovic to the European Community. Then the European Community had made conditional to have this referendum, which was held on 29th February and 1st March. A few days later the President declared, after the results came out -- declared Bosnia's independence and it was then recognised a few weeks later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Thank you for your comments, your Honour. Please, you said and indicated in your report that the ethnic composition of Bosnia was 43 per cent Muslims, 30 or 31 per cent Serbs and 17 per cent Croats, and the rest were others. You also said that the result of the referendum was that 66 per cent of the voters voted at the referendum, and out of that 99 per cent of those voted in favour of independence. In your view, on the assumption that all Muslims voted for independence, and it is not possible for all of them to vote, and that all the Croats actually voted, and that too is not possible, nevertheless a large number of Serbs at the referendum voted for independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, because I cannot say according to nationality, but 100 per cent minus 31 per cent is 69 per cent, and 66 per cent participated. So I cannot exactly say how many Muslims and Croats exactly participated -- how many Yugoslavs, members of other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: But in any event a good number of Serbs voted for independence, maybe more than half, but in any event if we exclude all the Croats and all the Muslims, nevertheless it emerges that a large number of Serbs voted for independence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how many Serbs voted in favour of independence. You can also turn the argument the other way round and say if we assume that all the Serbs did not participate, then we reach a 69 per cent, then there are 3 more per cent besides 31 per cent of Serbs who did not vote. I think it cannot help us in understanding these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I will not insist. Please, from your testimony in response to my questions and the questions by my learned colleague, it emerges that the first question that arose was the question of independence or not independence for Bosnia; is that correct, even before this other question of cantonisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Does it follow from what you have said that a distinction must be made, a clear distinction? Bosnia as a state and as a people did not aspire to independence, but it did not want to remain in some sort of Yugoslavia from which its most important and most powerful members, strongest members would withdraw; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: So Bosnia decided in favour of independence because it did not want -- or rather it took advantage of the right recognised it by the Badinter Commission to remain independent, and it did not want to join forces with anyone else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: In the course of the disintegration of Yugoslavia, when the Badinter Commission said that every republic had the right to decide what it would do, Bosnia decided to opt for independence and it did not want to join with anybody else; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only have some questions on the constitution. You stated that in early April 1992 there was a constitutional confusion that ensued. I think you called it "constitutional confusion". Okay. I will quote you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I clarify before you quote maybe? I did not intend to say that the constitution was confused. I wanted to say -- I wanted to explain that the way the constitution was implemented was confusing. Some provisions were implemented. Others were obviously not implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you read the quotation? You have read the quotation which you commented upon, because it appears you understand each other without knowing what the other one was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You speak the same language! MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): We did understand each other regarding this quote. What I would like to do is actually if you could explain to me, you said that the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a state within Yugoslavia. That was before, and it had its own constitution. Therefore, when it proclaimed its own independence, it had its own basic document, and this document, the constitution, provided that certain rights were given over to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Is it not true that by the proclamation of independence these rights were taken back by this republic, in other words there was no reason for any kind of confusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was confusion as to which Articles were implemented and as to which laws were implemented. I will give you only one example. This is the example of the unified armed forces. Of course, the laws continue to state that the Bosnian Army was the army of all three people, but, in fact, it appeared not to be the army of all three people, because there appeared two other armies at least. There appeared the Croat army, the HVO, and there appeared the Bosnian Serb army. So I can say from a legal point of view there was no confusion but on the ground with implementation there was. Many Articles were simply not followed and they were simply not implemented. This is all that I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that within the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina no Serbs or Croats participated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not want to say this. There participated Serbs or Croats, but the Serbs as well as the Croats established very powerful own military structures and armed forces' headquarters and they took also their own decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: I am talking of the bodies within the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the events that were controlled by the regular authority and the legal authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You mentioned that one way of disintegration of Bosnia-Hercegovina was the establishment of the so-called communities and autonomous regions on the part of the Serbs, that is Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is that correct? Is it correct that Bosnia-Herzegovina during the time of peace had a centralised government in Sarajevo and 109 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the contacts and communication between such a number of municipalities and the central government posed some difficulties? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina did provide the possibility of creation of communities, that is communities of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, cooperation municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in both cases both Serbs and Croats by establishment of the Serb autonomous regions and the Croatian community were referring to these Articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Constitutional Court ruled that there is no constitutional basis for establishment of such communes or communities as were created, and that such decisions on establishment of these communities were made null and void? Is it correct that the establishment of such communities was illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was a referendum provided for in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in other words that a referendum on certain issues could be called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think yes, but I have to check on which conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in all cases the results of the referendum were binding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly how it was. I would have to check this exactly, but the referendum was anyway -- if you mean the referendum on the independence -- it was a condition by the European Community, and so it was considered to be binding. The outcome of this referendum was considered to be binding. So accordingly the ministers of the European Commission then took their decision to recognise Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: In other words, the decision taken from the referendum, according to you, was binding for all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again this is a legal question. The Badinter Commission was aware of the problem that one third of the population was evidently not in favour of independence, and this was a problem, and I am not in a position to say whether or not it was legal or illegal to hold this referendum to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. Were there any negative votes will go in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were something like 99 per cent in favour but only 66 per cent of the voters had actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Were there any negative votes also cast? In a referendum the usual question is "yes "or "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there were 99 "yes", then maybe 1 per cent "no" or one per cent unclear or not valid, or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe some people were not clear and so they abstained from voting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people were not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So they abstained from voting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were against and so they did not participate in voting. This was their expression of being against. They did not recognise they have had to have a referendum on independence. So only two thirds of the population took actually part in this referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what I asked you. Were there any negative votes on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were 99 per cent "yes" from 66 per cent participants. In other words, there was a boycott of this referendum by one-third of the population. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): I do not want to repeat questions by my colleague which you answered, but is it correct that Bosnia-Herzegovina by proclaiming its independence had its own constitution and created its own legal system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment, your Honours. The issue of the cantonisation of Bosnia. Earlier you said that it was not raised at the same time as the independence issue. I mean, that is my understanding of what you said. When was this issue raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The issue was being discussed throughout the year 1991, but the first written proposals and the first maps were submitted by the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Where were those discussions held? Were those discussions held in an elected representative body within the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and were these issues discussed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were mostly discussed outside of the Assembly. They were discussed exactly in the framework of the peace conferences set up by the European Community, and the parties or those who perceived themselves being parties to this discussion submitted their own proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: In other words, the representatives elected in the 1990 elections did not raise that issue and did not discuss that issue in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appeared to the outside, to the members of the international community that these issues could not be settled within the elected bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the parties could not find a compromise, and this is why they offered their services and they set up this conference and they set up the Badinter Arbitration Commission, and they started other activities as a third force or in this case maybe a fourth neutral force just to help mediate between these different streamings and views and opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to thank your Honours, and this concludes my cross-examination. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we will have to have a break now and come back at 4.15 to continue with the next line of cross-examination. (3.45 pm) (Short break) (4.15 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is still on oath: MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): One question, your Honour; just a question, please. I would like to remind you that this morning the witness said, when asked on several questions, that she would supply the documents on the basis of which she composed the document number 50, and should I need, I would be allowed to ask additional questions, if necessary. Since several breaks later, I still have not been provided with these documents, I would just like to ask a question of the witness whether these documents are available for my review now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, we have observed the witness has been on the witness seat apart from the lunch period. I do not know if she can still provide it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can enlighten you on this one. We have this document here, even in copies. We can hand them over to Mrs Residovic at any moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can now do so. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we now hear you, Mr Brackovic, in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Good afternoon, your Honours. Good afternoon, Ms Calic. My name is Mustafa Brackovic. I am the defence attorney for Esad Landzo, and my co-counsel is Ms Cynthia McMurrey from the United States. Listening to your presentation yesterday and today I came to understand that you visited Yugoslavia on several occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went there many times. I spent a lot of time there in different parts of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you also in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was several times in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the last time that you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lost time was 1995, in the middle of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: If I notice correctly, you understand the languages of the populations of the former Yugoslavian territory, the Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also speak these languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I speak.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know both alphabets, both the Latin and the Cyrillic alphabets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know both.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report you stated that your report was based on your personal research on works of other scholars and specialists in this field, on the documents from the former Yugoslavia, on the reports by international organisations, documents, witness statements made available to you from the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, your report was made also based on witness statements provided by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used them as a background information. I tried not to use them as for the primary documentation, because I was not sure enough whether or not these witness statements are reliable. So I was trying to use as much as I could other documents, written documents, laws and reports, and statistics, such kinds, but I have of course in mind as a background knowledge what the witnesses were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: How many statements did you have available that you used during the time when you were preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no exact number, but it was a lot. It was quite a lot, many files, maybe hundreds of pages I went through, but I have not counted them.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give an approximate number? I do not insist on it, though.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I need to count them. I don't know, but it was quite a lot. It took me quite a long time to go through all these documents and statements.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these only the prosecution witness statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I actually don't know who exactly was a witness of the prosecution and who was exactly a witness of the defence. I used them as witness statements. I tried to explain I tried to use them the less possible.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Did these statements influence your report in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They gave me a background to what happened, especially what happened after the outbreak of the war, and it supported my already existing view that there was quite a difference between what I could find in the official gazettes and what I would find in the laws and in the constitution, and what was hatching on the ground. In that way it supported an already existing opinion about this gap between paper and reality.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: To what extent did they confirm or support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew from my research early on that many laws existed, and there existed a legal system and a constitution, but I knew already from my research and also from my personal experience of going to Yugoslavia in the middle of the war that the conditions on the ground were often very different from the legal framework.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: What were your conclusions from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot understand.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that certain issues -- constitutional issues and surrounding issues you found from that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My conclusion was and continues to be that we have to be very careful when we assess and when we analyse concrete events and that there was a big difference from between different areas, and we cannot conclude from what happened in one area, and we cannot assume that exactly the different things were happening in another surrounding. So there were big, big differences between certain areas. This confirmed what I knew before, and I think it was confirmed also by what went on in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the things you said in your report was based on writings and other scholars and specialists in this field; so is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Was your report based, among other things, on the written statement of Dr Andrew James William Gow, also given before this Tribunal in the case Prosecutor v Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know this statement by James Gow and I knew him before and I knew quite a lot of his writings. I used his writing as for the role of the JNA in this conflict, but he is one of several scholars which I quoted in my report, but I am familiar with the report of James Gow in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the contents of his testimony before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the written report.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Taking into account his testimony, it also formed the basis of your report that is here before us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In certain areas. His testimony was on a different area. It was Prijedor, and this is on Northern Herzegovina. As for the role of the JNA I used his writings, as I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: In the part that is applicable to this case, do you agree with everything that Dr Gow testified to and stated before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer in this general way. You should propose me concrete facts or events or what he said, opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will try to rephrase this question: there are no major discrepancies between your report and the report of Mr Gow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say that he is completely wrong, and I cannot see in a very general way that he is always right. We have to verify this in concrete detail.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, there are different views propounded by you and by Professor Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. We have to verify it. We cannot say it in such a general way. If you tell me which assumption or opinion or part of his expertise you are referring to, then I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: We will have occasion to refer to that in the course of this cross-examination, to verify the positions of Dr Gow and your own, but before starting the cross-examination I wanted to hear your general view on whether there are certain differences or not, and if there are, whether they have to do with certain minor differences or different views on certain events and situations of importance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The case on which Dr Gow was testifying was different from this one. It was a different geographic area. Therefore I do not know what his opinion would be on that case and on that area, so there might be differing views but there might also be complete agreement on what was going on. I simply don't know. I would have also to ask him himself what his opinion is on this specific event -- on the specific events in this area. He testified on another area.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that Dr Gow did not testify about this area. I know that very well. He testified on the macro situation in the territory of the municipalities of Prijedor. However, most of his testimony and his findings are based on the general conditions, the circumstances, that is the background of the conflict, the war and aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct? I would be so bold as to say that at least 80 per cent of his report has to do with the background. That is the same theme that you studied here yourself. If you wish, you have here the statement of Dr Gow, and I can put it at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with the statement of Dr Gow. However, I believe that the case is very different and his statement was written to support or to help to understand a certain case. It was not written to support or to help to understand another case, and maybe we should ask Dr Gow himself. I cannot answer for him if he would write exactly the same report, if he had to testify about this on-going case. So I cannot say if I can challenge or support everything what he said and what he wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but when talking about the background, what is common to all cases, would the findings of all expert witnesses who will be appearing before this Tribunal -- should they be concordant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I thought you were cross-examining this witness. Are you making your own propositions? If it is cross-examination, ask her questions relating to what her own expertise is. If you want to compare her own expertise with that of Gow, you can do so. Do not go about asking her to adopt him, what she wants to do, whether she did not adopt him. Why should she? She is an expert with respect to her own field. You have spent so many minutes getting nowhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And she is quite right. You have must refer to a particular passage on which you want her to either agree to or disagree with Dr Gow. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I am not asking the witness to say whether she accepts or not the report of Dr Gow. That is the free choice of the witness, but through the cross-examination that I will be embarking upon now I will check certain facts and events which appear in both testimonies, but before I embark upon that, I wanted first to check on the position and views of this expert witness. Thank you. Allow me to continue. I will not dwell any longer on these matters. May I just ask a question regarding what I have already asked you about? When you used the statements from the prosecution, the statements of witnesses, that you do not know whether they are witnesses of the prosecution or the defence, I understand that you need not know that. I would like you to tell me whether you knew whether the witnesses were Serbs or non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew whether they were Serbs or non-Serbs. It was indicated on the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there witnesses who were Bosnians or Muslims in the statements that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how many there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms Calic, you prepared two expert reports. I will not say that you did two expert reports, but I will say that two expert reports exist. The defence received the first expert report, dated March 3rd, 1997, and the second is dated March 7th, 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I did not send them out personally. There are some official procedures -- I am not familiar with how exactly these reports were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: You are not aware that there are two reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me help you. All counsel wants to know is whether you sent out two reports in respect of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I sent -- I prepared one report, but I think I made some minor corrections. I made some minor corrections. They were not two different reports. This was one report, but there had to be corrected a few passages or few sentences or words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this meets your question. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Yes. Yes. I simply wanted to check, because I have two reports, one dated 3rd March and the other 7th March. I wanted to see why I also noticed that there were minor corrections. So I simply wished to check with the witness which report should serve as a basis for my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a perfectly proper question. We should rely on one of the reports. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): You stated, Ms Calic, on page 4, the one but last paragraph of your expert report, that after the outbreak of the first armed conflicts in the summer of 1991 in the former Yugoslavia, the JNA became a Serb-dominated force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you thinking primarily of the officer personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only, but also the officer personnel, because -- I know what you want to ask me -- because already before the Serbs were already present in the officer corps. This is maybe what you want me to refer to, but after the outbreak of the war in the former Yugoslavia also many non-officers, non-Serbs, left the JNA. So it became more and more a Serb-dominated army.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask was such a situation not present even before 1991, that is that the officer corps in the former JNA was dominated by the Serbs to a high degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before 1991 Serbs were over-represented in the officer corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "over-represented", does that mean that they were dominant in relation to their share in the total population of former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were over represented. They maybe dominated. This is a question of -- can be discussed. For sure they were over-represented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why are you avoiding the word "dominant"? What you are saying amounts to the same thing: if they are over-represented, they necessarily must be dominant. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): As far as the intermediary and lower levels of the officer corps, were the Serbs represented with about 60 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to check the numbers. I do not know them by heart exactly, all the ranks and all the levels of this army.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Was the share of Croats 12.6 per cent before 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to check these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: And the Muslims' share was 2.4 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I have to check these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If what I have said is correct, would that mean that the Serbs participated in the officer corps in a far higher percentage than was their share in the total population structure of Yugoslavia as it was then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs were over-represented in the officer corps, the JNA, which was -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to pass on to a different area. You stated here in this report that Serbian deputies withdrew from the joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in October 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: After that did they form their own Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to forming their own Assembly, did they all over Bosnia-Herzegovina form in municipalities, at the local level, parallel organs of authority, their own municipal assemblies, administration, the police and the like; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that they did that because they were not allowed to participate in the work of Parliamentary assemblies of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the municipalities, or was it done for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs claim that they did this because they could not accept that the Muslim and the Croat parliamentarians took the decision that Bosnia should become a sovereign and maybe also an independent state. So they were challenging the legitimacy of these decisions, and that is why -- at least this is what they claim -- this is why they left the assembly and why they created their own bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Serbs in the territory of the municipality of Konjic formed the Assembly of the Serbian People of the Municipality of Konjic and other bodies of authority and the administration, including an Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read this in some of the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: This circumstance, this event concerning the formation of the municipality of Konjic, is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did not understand you well. I read in some of the witness statements that the Serbs were forming their own crisis staffs and other institutions, but I again cannot say whether this is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will limit myself. Your only source of knowledge is the statements of witnesses that you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the Serb municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Are those witnesses of Serbian nationality whose statements you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember which nationalities told about that in his statement. I cannot remember. I would have to check, but I cannot also say whether these persons were right or not, and they may even appear here in court. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not expect you to say whether they were right or wrong. I just wish to know whether you are aware of this fact. I would like to go on to ask whether it is true that the Serbs took a decision on the verification of the proclaimed Serbian autonomous regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina on January 15th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I showed the document yesterday confirming this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Serbian autonomous region of Herzegovina consisted of the following municipalities: Bileca, Cajnice, Gacko, Kalinovik, Loubinje, Nevesinje, Rudo, Trebinje and Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You read it very quickly. Yes, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the Serbian autonomous region of Herzegovina was limited to or consisted only of the territories of these municipalities that I have named?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were making claim to a part of Konjic, and they also -- this territory was then afterwards also controlled by Serb troops, but I cannot say exactly when this was, but I saw maps from 1993, where parts of the eastern parts -- the eastern part was, in fact, under Serb -- was supposed to be a part of this Herzegovinian region which at this time was already Serb Republic or proclaimed Serb Republic. I cannot say exactly when and under which circumstances this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: That means that you are aware that certain parts of the municipality of Konjic were included in the Serbian autonomous region of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of when this was. I showed the document in which this fact was not mentioned. So I cannot exactly say. I have no document which shows me when and why, in which part of the Konjic municipality might have become a part of this Herzegovinian region.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the decision on Serbian territories of the Assembly of the Serbian people of the municipality of Konjic of 22nd March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: You never heard about it, that it existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw any document.

utterances.speaker: MR BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: It is the document that I have here, and I would like to show it to you, and I would like to have it translated so that the expert witness can comment on it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you exhibiting it? Are you exhibiting this document? MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Later the defence will tender it as evidence. We now just wish to show it to the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have it marked at this stage. Have it marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let the witness have a look at it first. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): The document is written in Cyrillic. That is why I asked the witness whether she speaks and understands the languages of the piece of former Yugoslavia and whether she knows both alphabets, including the Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That will be a private thing between the two of you. It is not within the Trial Chamber which should have its own language. We do not limit the communication between just two of you. There should be one for the consumption of others. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): If you wish, I could suggest that this document be interpreted by the interpreters in the booth and then the Trial Chamber will be familiarised with its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, they can as well interpret, but when you have any document you intend to put in evidence, you must make sure that you produce its counterpart in the language of the Tribunal. That is a better way. You just do not bring it so that it can be translated in here. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you for your advice, your Honours. In future we will proceed as you have suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we please have it read out and translated? We cannot follow your internal debate. We have to know what this is all about. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): I do not mind. I can easily read it and have it simultaneously interpreted. If the Trial Chamber allows, I shall be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are putting it now as both witness and counsel. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, please will you decide which is the correct way to deal with this problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The document is not in the language of the Trial Chamber and it is difficult to admit as it is. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. As my cross-examination will certainly take some time and we will not be able to complete it today, we will have occasion to come back to this document on Monday, when we continue the cross-examination. If I may be allowed, I will go on to other matters in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: For the time being, you had better withdraw your document until you are prepared to introduce it. You are not familiar with that procedure? MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours.
